The 50000293-001 is an electronic air cleaner from Resideo (Honeywell Home).

An electronic air cleaner does not strain particles out of the air — it charges them and then collects them on plates of the opposite charge. That is a different physics from media filtration, and it shows up in the numbers: this unit holds back 81% of particles in the 0.3–1.0 micron range, where a MERV 11 media filter in the same cabinet size manages about a third of that. Small particles are the ones that reach deep into the lungs and the ones a pleated filter is worst at.

The trade is maintenance. The collecting cells are washable and they have to actually be washed — an electronic cleaner that goes a year without service stops collecting and becomes an expensive empty box. Plan on pulling the cells a few times a heating season.

  • Manufacturer Part #: 50000293-001/U
  • Type: Electronic air cleaner

The 50053952-020 is a TrueFRESH ventilation timer from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 20 / 40 / 60 minute settings.

A push-button timer is how a ventilation system gets used on demand without being left running. Press it after a shower or while cooking and the ventilator runs for the chosen interval and then stops on its own — which is the part people do not do manually.

Modern construction is tight enough that air changes no longer happen by accident. Where an older house leaked its way to fresh air, a well-sealed one holds humidity, cooking odour and everything else until something moves it out on purpose — which is the job this button starts.

Wall-mounted, so it goes where people are rather than at the equipment. A ventilation system nobody can reach is a ventilation system nobody uses.

Used with: VNT5150, VNT5200.

The ARD10TZ is an automatic round zone damper from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 10 in diameter, 24 V.

In a forced-air zoning system the damper is the moving part. The zone panel opens the dampers for the zones that are calling, keeps the rest shut, and runs the equipment — so one furnace serves an upstairs that wants cooling and a basement that wants nothing without either room getting the other one’s air.

Power closed, spring open. The actuator drives the blade shut and a spring returns it open, so a damper that loses power or loses its actuator fails open. The zone may lose control, but the blower never ends up pushing against a duct that is sealed off — which is the failure that breaks things.

Size it by duct diameter, and count the total 24 V load before adding dampers to an existing panel. Every actuator draws while it drives, and a transformer that was adequate for three zones is not automatically adequate for five.

The actuator mounts side or top, which is what makes it installable in a joist bay where the pipe can only be reached from one side.

The C7089R1013 is a RedLINK wireless outdoor temperature and humidity sensor from Resideo (Honeywell Home).

RedLINK is the wireless link Resideo uses between a thermostat and the rest of the system. Instead of pulling a wire from the equipment to every sensor and module, the devices are enrolled to the thermostat or to a wireless adapter and talk to it directly — which is what makes a sensor in a room with no thermostat wire, or an outdoor sensor with no conduit to the attic, a realistic job rather than a demolition project.

Enrolment is the step that decides whether it works. Each device has to be added to the system at the thermostat or the adapter; a RedLINK device that has not been enrolled is inert, and one enrolled to the wrong system stays enrolled until it is cleared.

Outdoor temperature is what lets a thermostat do anything smarter than react. It sets the balance point where a heat pump hands over to auxiliary heat, it drives outdoor reset on hydronic equipment, and it is what puts an honest outside reading on the thermostat screen instead of one pulled off the internet for the nearest airport.

Rated -40 °F to 140 °F and 0 to 100% RH, condensing — it is meant to be mounted outside and left there. Put it on a north wall, out of the sun; a sensor baking in afternoon light reports a temperature the house never sees.

The CPRD10 is a constant-pressure bypass damper from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 10 in round.

A bypass damper is what keeps a zoned system from destroying itself. When only one small zone calls, the blower is still moving the air it was sized for and it has nowhere to put it: static pressure climbs, ducts boom, the coil freezes on cooling and the heat exchanger cooks on heating. The bypass opens against that pressure and returns the surplus.

This one is not motorized and has no wiring. A calibrated spring holds it shut and duct pressure opens it, so it reacts to the actual pressure in the duct rather than to a signal from the panel. Set the spring tension once at commissioning and it needs nothing after that.

Size the bypass to the smallest zone, not to the trunk — the case it has to handle is one small zone calling alone.

This is the damper on the outdoor air intake. A house tight enough to hold its heat is also tight enough to hold everything else, so controlled ventilation brings in measured outside air instead of leaving it to whatever leaks. The F100F1620 is a media air cleaner from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 16 in x 20 in, MERV 11.

This is the cabinet and the first filter together, not a filter on its own. It cuts into the return duct ahead of the furnace or air handler and gives the system a deep filter bed instead of the one-inch slot the equipment came with. Everything downstream — the blower wheel, the evaporator coil, the humidifier — stays cleaner, and a coil that stays clean keeps its capacity.

What MERV actually buys you. The scale runs 1 to 16 and it measures how much of the small stuff the media holds back. MERV 8 catches dust and lint; MERV 11 starts catching the particles that carry odour and smoke; MERV 13 reaches the fraction that matters to people with asthma or allergies. The catch is that finer media restricts airflow, and a blower fighting a filter it was never sized for runs hot, moves less air and costs more to run.

That is why the deep media cabinet exists. Spreading four to five inches of pleated media over a large face area gives enough surface that a high MERV rating can be reached without choking the system — which a one-inch filter in the return grille cannot do at the same rating.

Pressure drop here is 0.23 at 500 FPM, which is what lets this cabinet run MERV 11 media without starving the blower.

This is the cabinet and the first filter together, not a filter on its own. It cuts into the return duct ahead of the furnace or air handler and gives the system a deep filter bed instead of the one-inch slot the equipment came with. Everything downstream — the blower wheel, the evaporator coil, the humidifier — stays cleaner, and a coil that stays clean keeps its capacity.

What MERV actually buys you. The scale runs 1 to 16 and it measures how much of the small stuff the media holds back. The HZ311 is a TrueZONE forced-air zone panel from Resideo (Honeywell Home) — 3 Zone, 1 Heat/1 Cool.

Zoning is what you do when one thermostat cannot describe the whole house. The panel takes a call from each zone thermostat, opens that zone’s dampers, closes the others and runs the equipment at the stage the call needs — so the finished attic and the north bedroom stop fighting each other through a single stat in the hallway.

Two numbers decide which panel. Zones is how many separately controlled areas it handles — this one is rated for 3 Zone. Stages is how much of the equipment it can drive: 1 Heat/1 Cool. A panel with enough zones but not enough stages will run a two-stage furnace as though it were single-stage, and the equipment loses the efficiency that was paid for.

Individual zone fan control lets one zone run its fan without calling the others — useful where a room needs circulation rather than heat.

It works with a discharge air temperature sensor, which is the part that protects the equipment when a single small zone calls: the panel watches supply temperature and backs the equipment down before the heat exchanger overheats or the coil freezes.

This is the panel on its own. A working installation also needs a 24 V transformer sized for the panel and the dampers, and a discharge air sensor — the kit version of this part number includes both.

Count the dampers before sizing the transformer. Every actuator adds to the load, and the intermittent faults in a zoning system are usually a transformer running at its limit rather than the panel.

What MERV actually buys you. The scale runs 1 to 16 and it measures how much of the small stuff the media holds back. MERV 8 catches dust and lint; MERV 11 starts catching the particles that carry odour and smoke; MERV 13 reaches the fraction that matters to people with asthma or allergies. The catch is that finer media restricts airflow, and a blower fighting a filter it was never sized for runs hot, moves less air and costs more to run.

Fits: SpaceGard 2200, 2120, 2250, Lennox PMAC20, GeneralAire AC-1. Media cabinets are sold by nominal face size and several brands share the same one, which is why a filter with a Resideo part number is often the correct replacement in a cabinet that carries somebody else’s badge. Check the size against what came out.

The S688A1007 is an airflow sail switch from Resideo (Honeywell Home), with a 5 in wide sail.

A sail switch proves that air is actually moving before it lets something else turn on. The sail sits in the airstream; when the blower runs, the air pushes it and the switch makes. No airflow, no contact, and whatever the switch controls stays off.

On an air cleaner that is the whole point: the high-voltage cell should energize only while the blower is running. It is the same job on a humidifier or an UV lamp — proving the fan rather than trusting that the fan was commanded.

Mount it where the air is reasonably straight, not immediately at an elbow, and check that the sail swings freely once the duct is closed up.

The THM4000R1000 is a RedLINK wireless adapter from Resideo (Honeywell Home).

RedLINK is the wireless link Resideo uses between a thermostat and the rest of the system. Instead of pulling a wire from the equipment to every sensor and module, the devices are enrolled to the thermostat or to a wireless adapter and talk to it directly — which is what makes a sensor in a room with no thermostat wire, or an outdoor sensor with no conduit to the attic, a realistic job rather than a demolition project.

Enrolment is the step that decides whether it works. Each device has to be added to the system at the thermostat or the adapter; a RedLINK device that has not been enrolled is inert, and one enrolled to the wrong system stays enrolled until it is cleared.

The adapter is the piece that gives a system a RedLINK radio of its own. It mounts near the equipment or on the duct and becomes the point every wireless device enrols to — sensors, remote modules, portable comfort controls.

The UV2400U1000 is a single-bulb 24 V UV air treatment system from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 16 W.

Ultraviolet in the duct does one of two jobs depending on where it is aimed. Pointed at the evaporator coil it keeps the coil surface free of the mould that grows on any permanently wet metal — that is the job with the measurable payback, because a fouled coil loses capacity and the smell goes into every room. Pointed into the airstream it works on airborne organisms, which is real but limited by how long the air is in front of the lamp.

It is not a filter and does not replace one. UV does nothing about dust, dander or smoke; media and UV solve different halves of the problem.

Plan for an annual lamp change from the start — output in the germicidal band falls off well before the lamp stops lighting.
